title: Role of statins in non-small cell lung cancer treatment: a systematic review and meta-analysis

sections.abstract:
This systematic review and meta-analysis investigates the association between statin use and clinical outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients, focusing on the therapeutic potential of statins and their impact on patient prognosis.

The review includes a mix of prospective and retrospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials to assess the relationship between statin use and NSCLC outcomes. ROBINS-I tool was used for assessing risk of bias, ensuring methodological rigour.

A literature search was conducted across several databases, including MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE, Web of Science and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. The databases were searched from inception to June 2024.

Participants included adult NSCLC patients prescribed statins before or after diagnosis, with no restrictions on sex, age or disease stage. Interventions of interest were statin medications, typically used for hypercholesterolemia, and also investigated for anticancer properties. The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), with secondary outcomes including progression-free survival (PFS), cancer-specific survival and NSCLC recurrence.

Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers. Results were synthesised via a random-effects model, with forest plots illustrating HRs for OS and PFS.

The meta-analysis included 25 studies with 51 536 NSCLC patients. Statin use was associated with improved OS (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.85). A trend towards improved PFS was observed but did not reach statistical significance (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.07).

Statin use may improve survival outcomes in NSCLC patients. These findings support the potential therapeutic role of statins in NSCLC management and call for further clinical trials.

CRD42016047524.
sections.introduction:
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent form of lung cancer, representing a significant global health challenge due to its high morbidity and mortality rates. 1 Despite advances in treatment modalities, including surgery, chemotherapy and targeted therapies, the prognosis for NSCLC patients remains suboptimal, particularly for those with advanced-stage disease. 2 Consequently, there is an ongoing quest to identify novel therapeutic strategies that can enhance patient outcomes.

Statins, a class of drugs primarily prescribed for lowering cholesterol levels, have attracted growing interest in the field of oncology for their potential pleiotropic effects beyond lipid-lowering. 3 These effects include anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory and antiproliferative properties that may influence cancer progression and patient survival. 4 Statins have demonstrated promise in preclinical studies and clinical trials across various cancer types, suggesting a potential role in cancer therapy. 5

The proposition that statins may impact the survival of NSCLC patients has spurred extensive research efforts. However, the results from individual studies have been inconsistent, with some reporting a survival advantage associated with statin use while others do not. 6 Consequently, a comprehensive evaluation of the existing evidence through meta-analysis is crucial to elucidate the overall impact of statins on NSCLC patient outcomes.

In this study, we aim to investigate the association between statin use and clinical outcomes in NSCLC patients. Specifically, we compare the outcomes of NSCLC patients who have been prescribed statins before or after diagnosis with those who have not received statin therapy. The control group includes individuals who did not receive statin therapy or received a placebo. This comparison is crucial to determine whether statin use has a significant impact on survival outcomes in NSCLC patients.

This meta-analysis aims to systematically review and synthesise the available literature to assess the association between statin usage and critical clinical endpoints in NSCLC: overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), disease-free survival (DFS) and NSCLC recurrence. By pooling data from multiple studies, we seek to provide a more robust estimate of the potential benefits or lack thereof, thus offering valuable insights for both clinical practice and future research.
sections.methods:
The present study adhered to a predefined protocol registered in PROSPERO under the registration ID CRD42016047524. The detailed protocol has been published. 7 The methodology and reporting followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, 8 and the PRISMA checklist is shown in online supplemental table S1 . The databases were searched from inception to June 2024.

Given the nature of this study as a systematic review and meta-analysis, it was not feasible to involve patients or the public directly in the research process. Our analysis was based on aggregated data from previously published studies, and thus, did not involve patient recruitment or active participation.

Studies eligible for inclusion encompass both randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies. However, non-clinical studies, review articles, proceedings and case-control studies were excluded from consideration.

Patients diagnosed with NSCLC, irrespective of sex, were considered for inclusion. Diagnostic classification adhered to the 2011 WHO classification guidelines. 9

The use of statins was the intervention method of concern in this study, which means patients who have taken statins of any type or dose before or after the diagnosis will be included in the intervention group.

The control group included individuals who did not receive statin therapy or received a placebo, allowing for a comparison of outcomes between those who were exposed to statins and those who were not.

The primary outcome of interest in this study was OS, representing the time from the initiation of cancer diagnosis or the initiation of a specific cancer treatment to death from any cause. Secondary outcomes included PFS, CSS, DFS and NSCLC recurrence. These outcomes aimed to provide a comprehensive assessment of the association between statin use and various aspects of NSCLC prognosis. PFS is defined as the time from the start of treatment until disease progression or death. CSS is defined as the time from the start of treatment to death due to cancer. DFS is defined as the time from the end of treatment to the recurrence of disease. NSCLC recurrence is defined as the time from the end of treatment to disease recurrence.

A systematic literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE (PUBMED), EMBASE, Web of Science, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and ClinicalTrials.gov. This thorough exploration aimed to comprehensively gather relevant studies related to statin use and NSCLC outcomes.

The search strategy employed for the PubMed database is outlined in detail in online supplemental table S2 , providing transparency and clarity regarding the methodology applied in this study. The exploration for relevant studies extended beyond the initial database searches to include a thorough examination of reference lists in pertinent original studies, reviews and key journals. This study imposes no restrictions based on language or publication year, ensuring a comprehensive inclusion of relevant literature. For articles published in non-English languages, translation support will be sought from international investigators within our institutes. This approach aimed to eliminate language barriers and encompass a global perspective in our review.

The initial screening involved an evaluation of titles and abstracts by two independent reviewers (GL and FL). Subsequently, a comprehensive assessment of the full texts of the identified articles was carried out by the same reviewers. This detailed scrutiny aimed to verify adherence to inclusion criteria and address exclusion reasons. After independently extracting the data, GL and FL collaboratively resolved any discrepancies through direct discussion, ensuring a consistent and rigorous approach to the selection process. This iterative approach enhanced the reliability and thoroughness of study inclusion, fortifying the robustness of subsequent analyses.

Two reviewers independently assessed and extracted information from the included studies. When discrepancies between the data extracted by the two individuals were identified, a discussion would have been held, and the article’s content would have been reviewed again. Once the two reviewers had independently extracted the data without any discrepancies, the collected information was then subjected to statistical analysis.

This structured approach facilitated a comprehensive capture of key details: (1) study characteristics (author, year of publication, study design, setting, locations, patient enrolment strategies and sample size in both groups) and (2) participant characteristics (age, sex, ethnicity, smoking status, alcohol consumption, histopathological diagnosis, Tumour, Node, Metastases (TNM) stage, history of treatment, associated comorbidities, timing of statin administration, type and dose, comparator given, follow-up period). In instances where reported data were incomplete, reviewers took the initiative to contact the respective authors, ensuring an accurate synthesis. This rigorous data extraction process forms the foundation for robust analyses and meaningful synthesis in the subsequent phases of the study.

To gauge the methodological rigour of the included studies, the Risk of Bias in Non-randomised studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool 10 was employed. This innovative tool offers a comprehensive evaluation across seven domains of bias: confounding, selection of participants, interventions themselves, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, measurement of outcomes and selection of the reported result. Reviewers independently addressed signalling questions within each domain to ascertain the risk of bias. This evaluation allowed for an overall judgement on the risk of bias pertaining to the assessed outcomes. In cases where discrepancies arose during the review process, a resolution was sought through discussion and consensus between the two authors.

The meta-analysis employed a random-effects model. HRs were used to synthesise survival data, each accompanied by 95% CIs. For studies reporting multiple HRs (eg, unadjusted and adjusted), we prioritised adjusted HRs to minimise confounding bias. If adjusted HRs were unavailable, unadjusted estimates were used. The statistical results were presented using forest plots or data tables to illustrate the combined data from the random-effects model analysis.

In cases where data were incomplete or unclear within the included studies, proactive measures were taken to mitigate potential biases and maintain analysis integrity. Efforts were made to communicate directly with study authors when available data were insufficient or unclear. This aimed to obtain comprehensive information and fill potential gaps in the dataset. When direct communication did not yield sufficient information, appropriate data imputation techniques were considered. These methods estimate missing values using statistical approaches aligned with the data’s nature. A sensitivity analysis was calculated to assess the robustness of findings in the face of missing data. By systematically varying assumptions during imputation, this analysis examined the impact on overall results to gauge potential influences on study outcomes.

Heterogeneity in the included studies was systematically evaluated to understand the variability across different trials. A significant p value from Cochran’s Q test 11 suggests the presence of heterogeneity among the studies included in the meta-analysis. The I² statistic quantifies the proportion of total variation across studies due to heterogeneity rather than chance. Higher values indicate greater heterogeneity. I 2 values at 0–25%, 25–50% and 75–100%, respectively, were considered to have low, moderate and severe heterogeneity.

Reporting bias was addressed based on the number of studies included in the analysis. A funnel plot was used when the study count exceeded 10, and Egger’s test was employed for datasets with fewer than 10 studies.

Subsequently, Stata V18.0 software was employed for comprehensive data analysis. The pooled estimation of HR and their corresponding 95% CI was conducted using the random-effects model.

Planned subgroup analyses were undertaken to provide a nuanced exploration of the relationship between statin use and NSCLC outcomes. The predefined subgroup analyses were as follows: (1) associated comorbidity such as hyperlipidaemia, coronary heart disease, etc. (2) Disease stage. (3) Cancer subtype. (4) Treatment type: surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy. (5) The time points at which patients start to take statins: prediagnosis or postdiagnosis. (6) Study type: RCT and retrospective studies. (7) Comparator given: placebo or no treatment. For subgroup analyses, a univariate model was used to assess the impact of individual factors. This approach focuses on the effect of one factor at a time, providing a clear and straightforward analysis.

The study was planned to conduct sensitivity analyses to assess the influence of methodological quality, evaluated by the ROBINS-I method, 10 on the results. Additionally, the impact of both methodological quality and sample size on the robustness of review conclusions will be explored through further sensitivity analyses. We excluded studies rated as having ‘moderate’, ‘serious’ or ‘critical’ risk of bias according to the ROBINS-I tool and re-ran the meta-analysis to assess the impact on the overall results. On the other side, we excluded studies with sample sizes that were considerably larger than others and re-ran the meta-analysis to assess the impact on the overall results.

The confidence in the cumulative evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system. 12 This approach evaluates the quality of evidence and provides a transparent framework for making recommendations. The GRADE system considers factors such as study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. The quality of evidence was categorised into four levels: high, moderate, low and very low. High-quality evidence implies a high level of confidence in the observed effect, while low-quality evidence suggests uncertainty or limited confidence. The GRADE approach aids in translating the results of the meta-analysis into actionable recommendations, considering the strength and quality of the underlying evidence.
sections.results:
The initial search across major databases identified a total of 5095 records. After removing duplicates, the titles and abstracts of 3348 articles were screened. During the initial reading of the abstract and the preliminary screening process, 1356 articles were selected for a detailed full-text review. During the full-text review, studies were evaluated for adherence to the inclusion and exclusion criteria. This led to the exclusion of 1331 studies due to reasons such as inappropriate study design, irrelevant outcomes or insufficient data. Reasons for exclusion were documented for each study. The final selection comprised a total of 25 studies 913 36 involving 51 536 patients that met the criteria for inclusion in the meta-analysis. Among the 25 included studies, there are 22 retrospective studies, two RCTs and one cohort study. The flowchart illustrating the study selection process, as recommended by the PRISMA statement, is presented in figure 1 .

Data extraction was performed according to the research plan. In the process of data extraction and analysis, we encountered some missing data. To address these missing data, we attempted to contact the original study authors via email to obtain the missing information. When this approach was unsuccessful, we marked the missing information as ‘unknown’ in our dataset. It should be noted that in the study by Maimon et al , 23 the 95% CI was derived using a method recommended by the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, 37 as the study only reported the HR and the p value. In the studies by Fiala et al , 16 Omori et al 9 for OS and PFS, Rossi et al 28 for OS and Walls et al 34 for OS, as well as in the study by Hung et al 19 for PFS, the HR and 95% CI were not directly reported. Instead, these values were estimated from the survival curves using methods described in the literature. 38 Due to the aforementioned missing data and other issues, the risk of bias for these articles was assessed as unknown. In the study by Ung et al , 31 data for squamous-cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma were initially reported separately. To obtain the final HR and 95% CI for the overall analysis, we applied a fixed-effects model to pool these two datasets. In the study by Zaborowska et al , 35 the HR and 95% CI for OS were provided for various follow-up periods, with this analysis selecting the values corresponding to the longest follow-up period, which is 5 years. The characteristics of the included studies, such as author, year of publication, study design, locations, sample size in each group, TNM stages, histology and therapy are summarised in online supplemental table S3 .

Two reviewers used the ROBINS-I method 10 to assess the methodological quality of the study. The evaluation included confounding, selection of participants, interventions themselves, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, measurement of outcomes and selection of the reported result. Out of the 25 studies included in the meta-analysis, two were categorised as having a high risk of bias, 12 as low risk and three as moderate risk. The remaining studies were labelled as having an unknown risk of bias. The detailed risk of bias assessment for each study is presented in figure 2 .

The primary outcome of interest in this meta-analysis was OS among NSCLC patients who used statins. The OS meta-analysis included data from 23 studies, with a total of 50 373 participants. The pooled HR for OS, calculated using a random-effects model, was 0.77 (95% CI: 0.70 to 0.85). The forest plot illustrating individual study estimates and the overall effect size is presented in figure 3 . The heterogeneity across the studies was assessed, and the I² statistic indicated 87.0%, suggesting a high level of heterogeneity.

The meta-analysis of PFS, including data from eight studies, demonstrated no significant impact of statin use on PFS in NSCLC patients (overall HR=0.87), (95% CI: 0.71 to 1.07). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across the studies (I² = 68.6%). The forest plot in online supplemental figure S1 showcases the results of various studies that reported PFS, as well as the overall effect size.

The forest plot displaying the HR for cancer recurrence, as reported in two studies, is presented in online supplemental figure S2 , showing a pooled HR of 0.77 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.08) with an I 2 of 0, suggesting no heterogeneity among the study results.

CSS data, reported in just four articles, were analysed and the result was an HR of 0.79 with a 95% CI from 0.62 to 1.00. The I² statistic was 90.0%, indicating high heterogeneity among these studies. This analysis is graphically represented in online supplemental figure S3 .

For DFS, no eligible studies reporting this outcome were identified, thus precluding the conduct of a meta-analysis. Consequently, an assessment of the association between statin use and DFS outcomes could not be performed based on the available literature.

Table 1 summarises the findings for primary outcome and secondary outcomes, providing a comprehensive overview of the meta-analysis results.

The study only provided the HR and p value, from which the 95% CI was calculated using a method recommended by the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. 37

The actual HR values were not provided in the study; instead, they were derived from the survival curves as per the methods described in the literature. 38

In the study, data for squamous-cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma were published separately. To obtain the final HR and 95% CI for the overall analysis, we applied a fixed-effects model to combine these two sets of data.

The HR and 95% CI were extracted from the data of the longest follow-up period.

UR, Unreported.

The assessment of reporting bias for OS and PFS involved distinct methods. The funnel plot for OS, displayed in online supplemental figure S4 , showed a symmetric distribution, which suggests minimal publication bias. Additionally, the Egger’s test for PFS, presented in online supplemental figure S5 , yielded a p value of 0.285, indicating no significant evidence of small-study effects.

Subgroup analyses were planned as follows: (1) associated comorbidity such as hyperlipidaemia, coronary heart disease, etc. (2) Disease stage. (3) Cancer subtype. (4) Treatment type: surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy. (5) The time points at which patients start to take statins: prediagnosis or postdiagnosis. (6) Study type: RCT and retrospective studies. (7) Comparator given: placebo or no treatment. But, in fact, some subgroup analyses cannot be performed because the information of patients included in studies is complex or some information is not reported. Only number 4 (treatment type), 5 (timing of statin administration) and 6 (study type) had sufficient information to allow for meaningful subgroup analyses.

The subgroup analysis of OS by surgery status revealed significant variations. For studies with an unknown proportion of surgery, the overall effect favoured statin use significantly (HR=0.77, 95% CI: 0.70 to 0.85, p<0.001, I² = 87.0%). Across all surgery types, there was a significant overall effect favouring statin use (HR=1.05, 95% CI: 0.67 to 1.65, p=0.012, I² = 77.4%). For partial surgeries, the overall effect favoured statin use significantly (HR=1.39, 95% CI: 1.01 to 1.92, p<0.001). The specific results are shown in online supplemental figure S6 .

The subgroup analysis of OS based on the use of chemotherapy demonstrated the following outcomes. For studies with no chemotherapy, the overall effect favoured statin use significantly (HR=0.93, 95% CI: 0.58 to 1.49, I² = 0.0%, p<0.001). Across all chemotherapy types, there was a significant overall effect favouring statin use (HR=0.74, 95% CI: 0.57 to 0.95, I² = 74.1%, p<0.001). For studies focusing on partial chemotherapy, the overall effect favoured statin use significantly (HR=0.86, 95% CI: 0.73 to 1.01, I² = 95.8%, p<0.001). The forest plot is shown in online supplemental figure S7 .

The subgroup analysis of OS based on the timing of statin administration relative to cancer diagnosis yielded the following results (shown in online supplemental figure S8 ). Studies where statins were administered before cancer diagnosis showed a significant overall effect favouring statin use (HR=0.76, 95% CI: 0.63 to 0.92, I² = 70.4%, p=0.009). For studies where statins were administered after cancer diagnosis, the overall effect favoured statin use significantly (HR=0.79, 95% CI: 0.57 to 1.08, I² = 96.7%, p<0.001). In studies with an unknown timing of statin use, the overall effect significantly favoured statin use (HR=0.78, 95% CI: 0.67 to 0.91, I² = 80.0%, p<0.001).

The subgroup analysis of OS based on the study type (research type) showed the following results: 20 retrospective studies exhibited a significant overall effect favouring statin use (HR=0.77, 95% CI: 0.69 to 0.85, I² = 88.6%, p<0.001). Three prospective studies demonstrated a significant overall effect supporting statin use (HR=0.82, 95% CI: 0.54 to 1.24, I² = 30.7%, p=0.236). Detailed results are shown in online supplemental figure S9 .

In the subgroup analysis by surgery status for PFS, significant variations were observed. Studies with an unknown proportion of surgery showed a significant overall effect favouring statin use (HR=0.63, 95% CI: 0.36 to 1.11, I² = 76.4%, p=0.014). Across all types of surgery, statin use was favoured with a significant overall effect (HR=1.38, 95% CI: 1.04 to 1.84, I² = 0.0%). For no surgeries, statin use significantly favoured the overall effect (HR=0.87, 95% CI: 0.66 to 1.13, I 2 =43.9%, p=0.148). These results are detailed in online supplemental figure S10 .

When based on the use of chemotherapy, the subgroup analysis for PFS demonstrated the following. Across all chemotherapy types, there was a significant overall effect favouring statin use (HR=0.81, 95% CI: 0.61 to 1.06, I² = 49.8%, p=0.093). Studies focusing on partial chemotherapy also significantly favoured statin use (HR=0.93, 95% CI: 0.89 to 0.97, I² = 0.0%). The forest plot for this analysis is provided in online supplemental figure S11 .

The subgroup analysis concerning the timing of statin administration relative to cancer diagnosis for PFS yielded the following results (as shown in online supplemental figure S12 ). Studies where statins were administered before cancer diagnosis indicated a significant overall effect favouring control (HR=1.38, 95% CI: 1.04 to 1.84, I² = 0.0%). After cancer diagnosis, statin use significantly favoured the overall effect (HR=0.95, 95% CI: 0.83 to 1.09, I² = 17.2%, p=0.299). In cases with an unknown timing of statin use, the overall effect was significantly in favour of statin use (HR=0.65, 95% CI: 0.52 to 0.81, I² = 0.0%, p=0.443).

Lastly, the subgroup analysis based on the study type for PFS showed that five retrospective studies had a significant overall effect favouring statin use (HR=0.86, 95% CI: 0.67 to 1.11, I² = 74.6%, p=0.003). Similarly, three prospective studies indicated a non-significant overall effect (HR=0.87, 95% CI: 0.52 to 1.46, I² = 69.0%, p=0.040). The detailed results of this analysis can be found in online supplemental figure S13 .

In studies categorised with an unknown bias level, the HR of OS spans from 0.62 to 0.83, with a combined HR of 0.72, indicating a significant protective effect. Heterogeneity is minimal (p=0.204, I² = 29.3%). For studies classified under a moderate bias level, two studies suggest a HR of 0.81, 95% CI: 0.57 to 1.16, with moderate heterogeneity (I 2 =54.6%, p=0.138). In the low bias level subgroup, studies consistently report a HR of 0.84, indicating a protective effect, and high heterogeneity is observed (I 2 =92.3%, p<0.001). Within the high bias level category, studies exhibit HR values ranging from 0.43 to 0.88, with no observed heterogeneity. The detailed content is presented in online supplemental figure S14 .

In studies with an unknown bias level category for PFS, the HR 95% CI ranges from 0.41 to 0.92, culminating in a combined HR of 0.62, which suggests a significant protective effect of statins. The heterogeneity observed in this subgroup is minimal, with a p value of 0.231 and an I² statistic of 30.3%. Moderate bias level studies, represented by a single study, indicate a HR of 1.05 (95% CI: 0.59 to 1.88), and moderate heterogeneity is observed in this category. Studies with a low bias level consistently report a HR of 0.95, suggesting a trend towards a protective effect for statins; however, this did not reach statistical significance, with low heterogeneity being observed. High bias level studies show a range of HR values from 0.26 to 0.91, also with no observed heterogeneity. The detailed content, including the forest plot, is presented in online supplemental figure S15 .

In the sensitivity analysis based on sample size (whether exceeding 1000), the subgroup with a sample size less than 1000 demonstrates a combined HR of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.70 to 0.97) indicating a significant protective effect. Studies with a sample size exceeding 1000 exhibit a combined HR of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.62 to 0.82), also suggesting a protective effect. Tests of effect size across sensitivity analyses based on sample size thresholds reveal significant differences. Heterogeneity is present in both sensitivity groups, with the group including studies with sample sizes of 1000 or more exhibiting high heterogeneity (I 2 =93.4%, p<0.001) and the group with sample sizes less than 1000 also showing high heterogeneity (I 2 =74.2%, p<0.001). The specific details and visual representation of the effect size tests and observed heterogeneity are depicted in online supplemental figure S16 .

In the sensitivity analysis for PFS based on sample size, the subgroup with a sample size less than 1000 demonstrated a combined HR of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.61 to 1.14), indicating a significant protective effect of statin use. In the subgroup with a sample size of 1000 or greater, there was only one study available, which reported a HR of 0.93 (95% CI 0.89 to 0.97). Due to the solitary study in this category, the heterogeneity (I²) could not be calculated, and the generalisability of the findings from this subgroup is limited. Significant differences were observed in effect size tests between sensitivity analyses based on sample size thresholds. The subgroup of studies with smaller sample sizes exhibited high heterogeneity at 73.0%. The detailed results, including the forest plot, are presented in online supplemental figure S17 .

The GRADE assessment for OS based on 23 observational and RCT studies suggests a moderate quality of evidence, with no serious risk of bias, indirectness, imprecision or publication bias. However, the evidence is marked by a significant degree of inconsistency, which may affect the overall confidence in the conclusions drawn for OS. For PFS, the evidence quality is very low, marked by serious inconsistency and imprecision. Although there is no serious risk of bias, indirectness or publication bias, the limited number of studies and issues related to heterogeneity and optimal information size contribute to the overall low confidence in the evidence. The details are displayed in online supplemental table S4 .
sections.discussion:
The current systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrate a significant association between statin use and improved OS in patients with NSCLC, with a HR of 0.77. This suggests that statin use is linked to better survival outcomes in NSCLC patients, potentially offering a new therapeutic strategy for this disease.

As a systematic review and meta-analysis, this article provides a comprehensive synthesis of prior published research, encompassing a significant patient population of 51 536 individuals from 25 studies, which substantially enhances the robustness of our findings. Recognising the challenges in conducting and finding RCTs, we also included observational studies to broaden the evidence base, offering a strength to our approach. In terms of potential reporting bias, our tests did not reveal any significant concerns. The study protocol was developed according to the PRISMA Protocols guidelines, 39 and the research was reported in accordance with the PRISMA statement, 8 ensuring transparency and high standards in the conduct and reporting of this systematic review. However, the study is not without its weaknesses. A notable challenge was the considerable heterogeneity observed among the included studies, which may be attributed to variations in patient characteristics, treatment regimens and the methodologies of the studies themselves. Despite our efforts to explore this heterogeneity through subgroup and sensitivity analyses, clear determinants remain elusive. Both subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were conducted without identifying any factors that markedly influenced the results. Additionally, the assessment of risk of bias using the ROBINS-I tool indicated several studies with an unknown risk of bias, which introduces uncertainty into the interpretation of our findings.

Despite the significant association between statin use and improved OS observed in our meta-analysis, the interpretation of these results should be tempered due to the considerable heterogeneity among the included studies. The potential benefits of statins on OS may be influenced by various factors, including differences in patient populations, treatment regimens and study methodologies.

The observed benefit of statin use on OS but not on PFS raises several important considerations. One potential explanation is that statins may exert their beneficial effects on OS through mechanisms beyond direct anticancer activity. For instance, statins are well-known for their cardiovascular benefits, which could indirectly improve survival outcomes in patients with NSCLC by reducing the risk of cardiovascular events that often coexist in this patient population. This cardiovascular effect may contribute to the observed improvement in OS, even in the absence of a significant impact on PFS.

Currently, numerous studies have demonstrated the potential benefits of statins in improving the prognosis of lung cancer patients. First, in terms of mechanism, statins may exert their beneficial effects through various pathways, such as inducing apoptosis, 40 overcoming resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, 41 enhancing the sensitivity of chemotherapeutic drugs 42 and inhibiting angiogenesis. 43 These mechanisms suggest that statins could potentially improve the prognosis of lung cancer patients. However, it is possible that the observed benefit in OS is not solely due to these anticancer mechanisms. The cardiovascular benefits of statins, such as reducing the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke and other cardiovascular complications, may play a significant role in improving OS. Second, in the realm of clinical research, the meta-analysis by Chen et al 44 included 13 observational studies and found that statin exposure was associated with better OS in lung cancer patients. Unlike our study, which focused on OS, Chen et al also analysed CSS but did not include PFS. Similarly, Xia et al 45 conducted a meta-analysis of 17 studies, showing that statins were associated with improved OS (HR 0.82, (0.76–0.88)). However, in their meta-analysis, statin use did not significantly improve PFS. In contrast, our results, which included a larger number of studies, demonstrated a statistically significant difference in PFS, indicating a different outcome compared with their study. Both Chen et al 44 and Xia et al 45 included various types of lung cancers in their analyses, and their results showed statistical differences in OS and PFS between NSCLC and SCLC. This highlights the importance of focusing on NSCLC in our study. Lastly, some studies have suggested that statins may reduce the incidence of lung cancer. A large-scale population-based study 46 found that the incidence of lung cancer was lower among statin users compared with the control group. However, Tan et al 47 conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the relationship between statin use and lung cancer risk, involving over 38 000 participants. Their results indicated no significant association between statin use and lung cancer risk, both overall and in subgroup analyses based on different drug types, dosages, duration of use and population characteristics. This topic, while related, is distinct from the focus of our study.

Our meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and updated assessment of the impact of statin use on survival outcomes in lung cancer patients. Compared with previous meta-analyses, which have shown mixed results, our study includes a larger number of studies and a broader range of outcomes. For example, while previous studies have shown no significant differences in OS between statin users and non-users, our analysis, which includes more recent studies, demonstrates a statistically significant improvement in OS and PFS. This suggests that the benefits of statin use may be more pronounced than previously thought.

This study has several limitations. Our meta-analysis included a total of 23 studies for the primary endpoint of OS, among which 21 were observational studies and two were RCTs. The predominance of observational studies in our analysis is a notable limitation, as observational studies may be subject to various biases, including selection bias and confounding factors, which can influence the results. While RCTs are considered the gold standard for evaluating treatment effects due to their ability to minimise bias, the limited number of RCTs included in our meta-analysis restricts our ability to draw definitive conclusions. Future research should aim to include more RCTs to strengthen the evidence base for the impact of statins on OS in lung cancer patients. The limited number of eligible studies for some secondary endpoints, such as CSS, DFS and PFS, introduces uncertainty and potential bias. With only eight studies contributing to PFS and the overall low quality of evidence, the findings for PFS should be interpreted cautiously, as they may not be as robust or reliable as those for other endpoints with more extensive data. Additionally, the inclusion of several retrospective studies in our meta-analysis may introduce publication bias, as studies with non-significant results may be less likely to be reported. Future research should aim to include a larger number of well-designed prospective studies to strengthen the evidence base for these endpoints. One notable limitation is the lack of eligible studies reporting DFS, which precluded a planned analysis of this outcome. Future research should aim to include studies that report DFS in patients with NSCLC treated with statins.

Despite the encouraging findings, our study raises several questions that warrant further investigation. The precise impact of statin therapy on PFS in NSCLC remains unclear due to limited data, and the optimal timing and selection of statin types for NSCLC treatment are yet to be established. Future research should prioritise well-designed, RCTs to evaluate the efficacy and safety of statins when used in conjunction with standard NSCLC treatment protocols. Additionally, there is a need for studies that explore the potential of precision medicine. Identifying patient subgroups that could most benefit from statin therapy is a critical next step. Research should aim to understand how genetic factors and specific statin types may act as modifiers of treatment response. This personalised approach, facilitated by genetic and molecular profiling, could lead to more targeted and effective statin use in NSCLC.

Future research should focus on elucidating the specific mechanisms through which statins exert their effects on survival outcomes in NSCLC patients. Well-designed RCTs that account for cardiovascular comorbidities and other confounding factors are needed to determine whether the observed benefits are primarily due to anticancer effects or cardiovascular protection. Additionally, studies should explore the potential for precision medicine approaches to identify patient subgroups that may benefit most from statin therapy.
sections.conclusion: This meta-analysis suggests that statin use may be associated with improved OS in NSCLC patients, but the evidence is subject to substantial heterogeneity. The lack of a significant impact on PFS suggests that the observed benefits may not be solely due to anticancer mechanisms. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify the specific contributions of statins to cancer outcomes and cardiovascular health in this patient population.
